Floating-point addition is not associative because real numbers must be represented with a finite number of bits. Modern processors generally use IEEE 754 formats, such as binary32 or binary64, in which each value has a sign, exponent, and limited-precision significand. When two floating-point numbers are added, the exact mathematical result is usually not representable in the destination format, so the hardware rounds it to a nearby representable value. The rounding error depends on the operands and, crucially, on the order in which additions occur.

For real arithmetic, the expressions (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) are equal. In floating-point arithmetic, the first addition in each expression may be rounded differently. For example, if a is very large and b is much smaller, adding b to a may have no effect because b lies below the precision available at a’s magnitude. If b is first combined with another number, however, their sum may become large enough to affect a. Cancellation between positive and negative values can make the discrepancy especially pronounced. Thus, even when every individual operation follows the standard correctly, changing the grouping can change the final result.

Large matrix multiplication exposes this issue because each output element is a dot product: many products are summed to produce one value. High-performance implementations rarely accumulate those products in a fixed left-to-right sequence. They divide matrices into tiles, distribute work across processor cores, vector units, or GPUs, and combine partial sums using parallel reduction trees. Different tile sizes, thread counts, scheduling decisions, instruction sets, or library algorithms can produce different reduction orders. Since each intermediate addition is rounded, those orders can lead to slightly different output entries.

Modern hardware can introduce further variation through fused multiply-add instructions, which compute a product and addition with only one final rounding, rather than rounding the product and sum separately. One implementation may use fused operations while another may not. Differences in precision, treatment of subnormal values, compiler optimization, and accelerator-specific arithmetic modes can also affect results.

These variations are usually small relative to the scale of the calculation, but they prevent bit-for-bit reproducibility. They may become noticeable for long dot products, poorly conditioned matrices, or sums containing values with widely differing magnitudes. They can also propagate through later computations and alter threshold decisions or convergence behavior. Reproducibility therefore requires deliberate controls, such as fixed reduction trees, consistent hardware and compiler settings, higher-precision accumulation, compensated summation, or specialized reproducible arithmetic. These measures often reduce performance, so numerical libraries commonly favor speed while promising results within an error tolerance rather than identical bits.
